answers.brief_reasoning: Random assignment to conditions with manipulated IV.
answers.final_answer: Experiment (randomized experiment with random assignment to Quiz vs. Reread conditions).
Retention = the number of the 20 vocabulary terms a student defined correctly on the written test one week later.
On average the Quiz group correctly defined about 3.3 more terms (14.2 vs 10.9 out of 20) than the Reread group, so the Quiz group retained more vocabulary one week later.

Informed consent/assent: parents gave written permission and each student gave verbal agreement (also told they could stop at any time without penalty). Alternatively, confidentiality: tests were labeled with code numbers instead of names.

Generalizability is limited. The participants were seventh graders from only two public middle schools in one mid-sized city, and they were volunteers (only students whose parents returned forms took part), not a random sample. So the results may not apply to other ages, regions, or types of schools. Random assignment supports a causal conclusion within this sample, but it does not make the results generalizable.

The findings support the hypothesis. The Quiz group's mean retention (14.2) was higher than the Reread group's (10.9), and the researchers reported that this difference was statistically significant, so it is unlikely to be due to chance. Because students were randomly assigned and both groups spent the same 10 minutes on their task, the higher retention can be attributed to taking the practice quiz rather than rereading.

answers.brief_reasoning: Variables measured, not manipulated; correlation computed.
answers.final_answer: Correlational study (non-experimental; sleep and mood were measured, not manipulated).
Each student's average number of minutes of sleep per night (time from falling asleep to waking, recorded by a wrist sleep monitor) across 14 school nights.

answers.brief_reasoning: Positive sign gives direction; 0.52 is moderate strength.
answers.final_answer: A moderate positive correlation: students who slept longer on average tended to report higher average morning mood. It does not show that more sleep causes better mood.

answers.brief_reasoning: Several guidelines appear in the study.
answers.final_answer: Informed consent/assent: researchers got a signed parent permission form and the student's own signed agreement before including anyone. Generalizability is limited. All participants were ninth graders from a single suburban high school, and only 240 of the 400 invited students took part (they volunteered by returning forms). answers.brief_reasoning: Positive r is consistent with the hypothesis.
answers.final_answer: The finding supports the hypothesis. Because the study is correlational, it shows an association, not proof that longer sleep causes better mood. Mood could affect sleep, or a third variable could affect both.

answers.brief_reasoning: 65% vs. 38% is a difference of about 27 percentage points.
answers.final_answer: A larger share of the Large-then-small group complied (65%) than of the Small-only group (38%). Shoppers who were first asked the large request agreed to the small request more often.

Generalizability is limited. Random assignment supports a causal conclusion within this sample, but the sample was not randomly drawn from a broader population.

The findings support the hypothesis. Shoppers who first refused the large request (10 hours a month) agreed to the five-minute request at a higher rate (65%, 52 of 80) than shoppers who were asked only the small request (38%, 30 of 80). Because shoppers were randomly assigned, the higher compliance is likely caused by the large request coming first. This fits the door-in-the-face technique.

answers.brief_reasoning: Random assignment to course vs waiting list with manipulated IV.
answers.final_answer: Experiment (randomized experiment with a waiting-list control group).
Test anxiety is a student's total score (20–100) on the 20-item questionnaire about anxiety before tests, where each item is rated 1 (never) to 5 (always). Higher scores mean more anxiety.

After four weeks the mindfulness group's mean was 54 and the waiting-list group's mean was 65, an 11-point gap. On average, students who took the course reported less test anxiety than students who had not taken it yet. Both groups started out about the same (68 and 67).

Informed consent. Students signed consent forms that described the course and the waiting list, and they were told they could stop at any time. (Other answers also fit: confidentiality, because questionnaires were identified by code numbers; or IRB approval.)

The findings are limited in how far they generalize. All participants came from one community college, and they volunteered after an announcement asking for students who felt anxious before tests. So they are not a random or representative sample. The results may apply to anxious community college students like these, but maybe not to students at other schools, students with low anxiety, or other age groups. Random assignment supports a causal conclusion within this sample, but it does not make the results generalizable.

The findings support the hypothesis. Students were randomly assigned, and both groups started with similar means (68 and 67). The mindfulness group's mean dropped by 14 points to 54, while the waiting-list group dropped by only 2 points to 65. Because the waiting-list group controls for time and retesting, the larger drop in the course group suggests the four-week course caused the reduction in test anxiety. One caution: the scores are self-reported and students were not blind to their group, so expectancy effects may have played a part.

answers.final_answer: A school district should ban students from using phones during class because phone notifications and checking divide attention and impair learning.

Source 1: students randomly assigned to have phones send notifications scored a mean of 66% on the lecture quiz vs 78% for students whose phones were off and stored in a bag; the difference was statistically significant.

Attention is limited. Divided attention (or multitasking) shows that when people try to attend to two things at once, they perform each one worse. Each notification pulls selective attention away from the lecture, so less of it gets encoded into long-term memory, and quiz scores drop. Because Source 1 used random assignment, the drop can be said to be caused by the phones. A ban would remove this distraction in class.
Source 2: 58% of 600 surveyed students said they check their phones at least five times during a typical class, and 71% of 120 teachers said phones distract students during lessons.

Operant conditioning explains this. Phones deliver rewards (messages, likes) on a variable-ratio schedule, which builds a habit that is very hard to extinguish. That explains why students check so often even during class. Willpower alone is unlikely to stop a behavior reinforced this way, so changing the environment with a ban removes the cue and the chance to be reinforced. This supports a ban.

answers.final_answer: High schools should not require community service hours for graduation, because requiring service turns it into an externally controlled task. That undermines students' intrinsic motivation to keep volunteering later.

Source 2: Students were randomly assigned to groups. Six months later, the Required group volunteered a mean of 4 hours by choice, compared with 9 hours for the Optional group. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Overjustification effect / intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation.
answers.final_answer: This fits the overjustification effect. When an external pressure (a graduation requirement) controls a behavior, people credit the behavior to that outside cause instead of their own interest, so intrinsic motivation drops. Once the requirement was gone, the Required students had less intrinsic reason to volunteer and gave fewer hours than the Optional students. Because students were randomly assigned, the experiment supports the conclusion that the requirement itself caused the lower volunteering. That supports not requiring service.
Source 3: Fifteen students who completed required hours described them as 'something I had to get done.'

Self-determination theory says lasting motivation depends on meeting the need for autonomy. Students who called the hours 'something I had to get done' saw the service as controlled and imposed on them, not chosen. In that case the behavior is not internalized and does not become a lasting habit, so a requirement is unlikely to build a long-term commitment to volunteering. (The source notes that interviewees may have had stronger opinions than others, so this evidence is only suggestive.)

review.summary: The bundle is generally workable, but the Source 3 evidence is weakly tied to the required-versus-optional question. Source 2 also has a possible confound, since the Required group had already served 20 hours.

scope_skill.notes: The content is within Unit 4 (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, social responsibility norm). Skills match the EBQ structure.

answers.brief_reasoning: Claim: Yes. Teachers should spread homework and review out over time (distributed practice) instead of concentrating it just before a test, because spaced study leads to better long-term retention than cramming.
answers.final_answer: Teachers should spread homework and review out over time, because distributed (spaced) practice gives better long-term retention than massed practice (cramming).

answers.brief_reasoning: Source 1 is a randomized experiment, so its result can support a causal claim.
answers.final_answer: Source 1: Adults who studied in three 20-minute sessions over three days recalled 33 words on average one week later. Adults who studied in one 60-minute session recalled only 21. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Use the spacing effect and the forgetting curve.
answers.final_answer: This result shows the spacing effect (distributed practice), which goes back to Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve. Each spaced session comes after some forgetting has happened. Retrieving and relearning the material at that point strengthens memory consolidation and moves the words into long-term memory. Both groups studied for the same total time (60 minutes), and people were randomly assigned to groups. So the better recall after a week can be traced to spacing itself. Spreading homework and review over time should likewise improve students' long-term retention.

answers.brief_reasoning: Use a different source from Part B.
answers.final_answer: Source 2: Classes randomly selected to take a short cumulative quiz every week averaged 84% on the same final exam. Classes with no weekly quizzes averaged 78%. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Use a different concept: the testing effect (retrieval practice).
answers.final_answer: This result shows the testing effect (retrieval practice). Recalling information from memory strengthens the retrieval cues and pathways to it, so it is easier to remember later. Weekly cumulative quizzes make students retrieve material again and again over the semester. This spreads retrieval out in time instead of saving it all for the end, which led to higher final exam scores. The same teachers taught both types of class, which controls for teacher effects as a confounding variable. This supports organizing review as spaced, recurring practice.

review.summary: The EBQ is well built overall but has structural and scoring defects that fail it under strict review, chiefly the rubric for C2 and E2 and the part and point structure of the EBQ.

answers.brief_reasoning: Claim: A company should not reward employees mainly with team-based bonuses, because team-only rewards encourage social loafing and feelings of unfair workload; individual bonuses (or individual accountability) should be primary.
answers.final_answer: A company should not rely mainly on team-based bonuses; it should reward mainly individual performance because team-only rewards reduce individual effort (social loafing).

answers.brief_reasoning: Source 1: students who believed only the team's total force was measured pulled a mean 78 units vs 100 units when individually measured, a statistically significant difference.
answers.final_answer: Source 1: Team condition mean force 78 units vs Alone 100 units (significant).

answers.brief_reasoning: Social loafing: when individual contributions are not identifiable, people exert less effort. Team-condition students pulled about 22% less because their own effort was hidden in the group total. Paying only team bonuses makes each worker's contribution unidentifiable in the same way, so effort drops, which supports rewarding individuals. Because Source 1 was an experiment, it shows cause and effect.
answers.final_answer: Social loafing explains the lower team effort; team-only bonuses hide individual contributions and so reduce effort, supporting individual bonuses.

answers.brief_reasoning: Source 2: among 500 employees, perceived unfair sharing of workload correlated r = +0.44 with burnout.
answers.final_answer: Source 2: r = +0.44 between perceived unfair workload and burnout.

answers.brief_reasoning: Equity theory / stress: workers who feel they give more than others for the same reward experience inequity, which acts as a chronic stressor (general adaptation syndrome, exhaustion stage) and leads to burnout. Team bonuses split rewards equally no matter how much each person contributed, so they encourage perceived inequity. The moderate positive correlation fits this. Limitation: correlation is not causation, and the volunteer sample is biased.
answers.final_answer: Equity theory/chronic stress: equal team rewards for unequal work create perceived inequity, which causes stress and burnout (correlational evidence only).

review.summary: The EBQ structure is sound and the sources are well written, but the part D/E key is internally inconsistent: the keyed answer for D and E points to Source 3, which is confounded, while the keyed concept for E (incentive/extrinsic motivation) is unsupported by Source 3. Parts C, D and E are also scored in ways that conflict with the stated skills. Details are in the notes below.

The E model answer (incentive theory, extrinsic reward) explains a sales difference that the source cannot attribute to the bonus type. Part E's alternative solution says burnout from unfair workloads supports the claim, but that is Source 2 evidence, not the part D evidence, so the rubric mixes sources. E2's accepted concepts (positive reinforcement, distress) are loose. Rubric row C2's common error ('uses the same concept as in the earlier part') is stale text in a part with no earlier part. Parts C and E carry skill code 1.A, while the item's target skill is 4.B, so the explanation parts do not assess the target skill.

stimulus_expression.notes: The table and source text are complete and clear. However, the Source 2 note that volunteers were more likely to work in teams that reward group results is odd and unused, and the sources do not support two clean, distinct claims.

distractor_explanation.notes: This is an FRQ, so there are no distractors. The common-errors lists are generic and partly stale.

exam_suitability.notes: The 7-point structure follows the official EBQ format. The model answers are overly one-sided and ignore the stated source limitations, which the official task would expect students to weigh.

Students must choose a defensible claim, cite specific evidence from a table or sources, and link it to a named AP concept (social loafing, diffusion of responsibility, correlation vs. causation, confounds, nonrandom assignment, sampling or volunteer bias, motivation). No calculation is needed. The scenario is not ambiguous, because any coherent claim is creditable if it is tied to evidence and a concept.
